questions.question: CTA shows an entry tear distal to the left subclavian artery, with retrograde extension into the ascending aorta. Which classification and initial definitive pathway are appropriate?
options: Stanford B; urgent descending-aortic TEVAR
Stanford B; anti-impulse therapy and surveillance
Stanford A; emergency open aortic repair
Stanford A; planned elective repair after stabilization
questions.explanation:
Anatomical Classification of Aortic Dissection

Correct answer: Stanford A; emergency open aortic repair

Classify the Extent

**Stanford depends on ascending involvement, not the entry-tear site.**

Any ascending involvement is A; B spares the ascending aorta. Isolated arch disease may require more detailed contemporary classification.

**Timing:** hyperacute <24 hours; acute 1–14 days; subacute 15–90 days; chronic >90 days.

Anatomical involvement and complications determine immediate treatment; duration is a separate classification axis.

Clinical Consequence

**Urgent surgical assessment and anti-impulse treatment proceed together.**

Medical stabilization is a bridge to repair, not a reason to defer an operable acute type A lesion.

**DeBakey describes origin and propagation.**

I originates in the ascending aorta and extends beyond it; II is confined to ascending; III originates in descending.

DeBakey III subtype | Extent

IIIa | Descending thoracic, above diaphragm

IIIb | Extends below diaphragm

Stanford B; urgent descending-aortic TEVAR: TEVAR is commonly used for complicated descending dissection; an entry tear there does not negate ascending involvement.

Stanford B; anti-impulse therapy and surveillance: This fits disease sparing the ascending aorta without complications; retrograde ascending involvement changes the Stanford category.

Stanford A; planned elective repair after stabilization: Elective repair suits selected stable chronic disease; acute ascending dissection carries immediate rupture, regurgitation and tamponade risks.

ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001106

questions.question: In type B dissection, renal hypoperfusion varies with pressure. CTA shows compression of the aortic true lumen across the renal ostium without a flap extending into the renal artery. What mechanism predominates?
options: Dynamic branch-vessel obstruction
Static branch-vessel obstruction
Renal artery thromboembolism
Atheroembolic renal disease
questions.explanation:
Dynamic and Static Malperfusion

Correct answer: Dynamic branch-vessel obstruction

Mechanism

**Dynamic:** false-lumen pressure compresses the true lumen and obstructs a branch origin.

Severity can change with the pressure relationship between lumina.

**Static:** the dissection propagates into the branch, producing fixed narrowing or thrombosis.

Treatment Implications

**Malperfusion makes type B dissection complicated.**

Urgent aortic-team treatment is needed; proximal tear coverage may restore true-lumen flow.

**Persistent branch obstruction may need fenestration or branch stenting.**

Monitor lactate, urine output, abdominal findings and limb perfusion; imaging anatomy alone does not quantify organ injury.

Static branch-vessel obstruction: Static obstruction results from dissection entering the branch with fixed stenosis or thrombosis; that branch extension is absent here.

Renal artery thromboembolism: An embolus creates a branch filling defect and generally fixed occlusion; ostial obstruction varying with true-lumen compression suggests a flap mechanism.

Atheroembolic renal disease: Cholesterol emboli affect small vessels, often with skin signs after instrumentation; this is major-ostial perfusion compromise.

ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001106

questions.question: A patient with Marfan syndrome has abrupt, severe tearing chest pain, equal pulses and normal blood pressure, with no new murmur or neurological deficit. What is the ADD-RS?
questions.explanation:
Aortic Dissection Detection Risk Score

Correct answer: 2

Scoring

**Count positive categories, not individual features.**

Marfan syndrome gives 1 for predisposition; abrupt/severe/tearing pain collectively gives 1; examination gives 0.

Use in Diagnosis

**A high-risk presentation requires definitive imaging.**

D-dimer is an adjunct in selected low-probability pathways, not a replacement for CTA in this case.

**A normal ECG or chest radiograph does not exclude dissection.**

Intramural hematoma, limited disease or thrombosed false lumen can complicate biomarker interpretation.

Category | Examples; maximum 1 point each

Predisposition | Heritable aortopathy, family history, known aneurysm, recent aortic manipulation

Pain | Abrupt onset, severe intensity, ripping/tearing quality

Examination | Pulse/BP differential, painful neurological deficit or new AR, shock

1: One point would apply if only one risk category were present; this patient has both a predisposing condition and high-risk pain.

3: Three requires a high-risk examination category as well; the supplied examination does not provide one.

4: ADD-RS is capped at three categories; multiple pain descriptors do not each contribute a separate point.

ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001106

questions.question: A hemodynamically stable patient has abrupt severe chest pain maximal at onset, an interarm pulse difference and a new diastolic murmur. ECG shows ischemic changes. Which investigation should be prioritized before committing to an antithrombotic or fibrinolytic ACS pathway?
options: Immediate invasive coronary angiography
Serial high-sensitivity troponin measurements
D-dimer-based exclusion pathway
Urgent CT angiography directed at suspected acute aortic syndrome
questions.explanation:
Acute Aortic Syndrome Can Present With Myocardial Ischemia

Correct answer: Urgent CT angiography directed at suspected acute aortic syndrome

Recognize Aortic Coronary Malperfusion

**Dissection can involve a coronary ostium**, producing ischemic ECG changes or troponin elevation without primary plaque rupture.

**Abrupt maximal pain, pulse asymmetry and new AR** create a high-risk aortic presentation; ECG and chest radiography cannot exclude it.

Select Definitive Imaging

**Urgent CTA of the aorta** is preferred in most stable patients; ECG gating improves proximal-aortic assessment.

**Bedside TEE** is particularly useful when transfer is unsafe; MRI is generally less practical in the acute emergency.

**Resolve the aortic diagnosis before an indiscriminate ACS antithrombotic/fibrinolytic pathway.** Begin monitoring, analgesia and urgent aortic-team coordination.

Immediate invasive coronary angiography: Coronary assessment may become necessary, but the abrupt pain, pulse discrepancy and new regurgitant murmur require urgent evaluation of the suspected aortic emergency.

Serial high-sensitivity troponin measurements: Troponin can identify myocardial injury but cannot exclude aortic dissection or establish whether coronary ischemia is due to aortic involvement.

D-dimer-based exclusion pathway: A low D-dimer can contribute in selected low-probability pathways, but this high-risk presentation requires definitive imaging rather than biomarker exclusion alone.

questions.question: A patient with suspected proximal dissection has shock and cannot safely leave the resuscitation area. An experienced echocardiographer is immediately available. Which test best provides rapid definitive proximal-aortic information?
options: Transthoracic echocardiography alone
Contrast-enhanced whole-aorta CT
Aortic magnetic resonance angiography
Bedside transesophageal echocardiography
questions.explanation:
Imaging an Unstable Suspected Aortic Dissection

Correct answer: Bedside transesophageal echocardiography

Immediate Information

**TEE assesses proximal flap, AR, tamponade and ventricular function.**

It can be performed bedside or in theatre while surgical management is organized.

Limitations and Complementary Imaging

**A negative study is not universally definitive.**

Distal ascending/arch blind regions and operator dependence matter; persistent suspicion requires further assessment.

**CTA maps the entire aorta and branches when feasible.**

ECG gating reduces proximal motion artifact; MRI is useful for selected stable patients and follow-up.

**Avoid delaying emergency repair** merely to obtain every imaging modality when diagnosis and operative need are established.

Transthoracic echocardiography alone: TTE quickly assesses effusion and regurgitation but incompletely visualizes the thoracic aorta; a negative result cannot exclude dissection.

Contrast-enhanced whole-aorta CT: CTA is preferred in most stable patients and maps branch anatomy; unsafe transfer makes bedside TEE the immediate choice.

Aortic magnetic resonance angiography: MRI offers comprehensive imaging without ionizing radiation but is impractical for an unstable patient requiring active resuscitation.

ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001106

questions.question: A hypertensive patient with uncomplicated acute type B dissection has HR 112/min and BP 186/104 mmHg, with preserved perfusion and no beta-blocker contraindication. What is the best initial pharmacological sequence?
options: Oral labetalol followed by oral amlodipine
IV nicardipine, then add esmolol after pressure normalizes
IV nitroprusside followed by oral metoprolol
IV esmolol, then add nicardipine if pressure remains high
questions.explanation:
Anti-Impulse Therapy in Acute Aortic Syndrome

Correct answer: IV esmolol, then add nicardipine if pressure remains high

Treatment Sequence

**Analgesia and arterial-line monitoring; initiate IV beta-blockade.**

Esmolol: 500 micrograms/kg over 1 minute, then 50 micrograms/kg/min; titrate to response, commonly up to 200 micrograms/kg/min.

**Add IV vasodilator if needed after rate control.**

Nicardipine ==5 mg/hour==; increase ==2.5 mg/hour== every 5–15 minutes, maximum ==15 mg/hour==.

Targets and Safety

**2022 ACC/AHA:** HR 60–80/min; SBP ==<120 mmHg== or the lowest pressure maintaining organ perfusion.

**Monitor bradycardia, AV block, bronchospasm and hypoperfusion.**

Shock, major malperfusion or acute severe AR requires individualized hemodynamic management rather than automatic target chasing.

Control pain and impulse → Reassess perfusion → Add vasodilator if required

Oral labetalol followed by oral amlodipine: Oral drugs suit longer-term control; the acute hypertensive tachycardic emergency requires titratable IV treatment and invasive monitoring.

IV nicardipine, then add esmolol after pressure normalizes: Nicardipine is useful after rate control; vasodilation first can provoke reflex tachycardia and increase aortic impulse.

IV nitroprusside followed by oral metoprolol: Nitroprusside is an adjunct after adequate rate control; oral beta-blockade does not provide the initial rapid titration needed here.

questions.question: A patient with acute type B dissection has active severe bronchospasm, HR 118/min and preserved LV systolic function, without shock or AV block. Which IV agent is the most appropriate alternative for initial rate control?
options: Nicardipine
Diltiazem
Nitroprusside
Amiodarone
questions.explanation:
Rate Control When Beta-Blockade Is Unsuitable

Correct answer: Diltiazem

Alternative Strategy

**IV non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockade** can substitute when beta-blockers are contraindicated or not tolerated.

Diltiazem or verapamil slows AV nodal conduction and reduces rate; titrate under continuous monitoring.

Patient Selection

**Preserved ventricular function and adequate pressure matter.**

Avoid this strategy in decompensated systolic failure, significant AV block or hypotension.

**Reassess pressure after rate control.**

Add a titratable vasodilator if needed; maintain organ perfusion and coordinate definitive aortic management.

**This acute alternative does not imply chronic preference** for calcium-channel blockers in every inherited aortopathy.

Nicardipine: Nicardipine lowers pressure but does not reliably suppress heart rate; it is added once impulse control is established.

Nitroprusside: Nitroprusside rapidly reduces afterload but may trigger reflex tachycardia; it does not replace initial rate control.

Amiodarone: Amiodarone treats selected tachyarrhythmias; this sinus tachycardia needs impulse control rather than antiarrhythmic conversion.

questions.question: A patient has confirmed acute type A aortic dissection, hemopericardium and tamponade. An emergency aortic surgical team is ready. Which definitive strategy is most appropriate?
options: Completely evacuate the hemopericardium percutaneously before aortic repair
Create a pericardial window, followed by staged aortic repair
Perform controlled small-volume pericardiocentesis before proceeding to aortic repair
Emergency aortic repair with operative management of the tamponade
questions.explanation:
Aortic Dissection With Hemopericardium

Correct answer: Emergency aortic repair with operative management of the tamponade

Definitive Source Control

**Type A dissection with tamponade requires emergency aortic repair.** Operative tamponade relief occurs with control of the bleeding source.

**Coordinate surgery, anesthesia, blood products and perfusion support.** A separate drainage procedure should not delay a ready aortic team.

Rescue Drainage Is Different

**Controlled minimal pericardial drainage** may bridge otherwise fatal tamponade when immediate surgery is unavailable.

**Remove only enough to restore essential perfusion**, often targeting approximately 90 mmHg systolic pressure in this rescue context.

**Complete decompression may accelerate bleeding.** A temporary pressure improvement neither repairs the aorta nor eliminates recurrent tamponade risk.

Completely evacuate the hemopericardium percutaneously before aortic repair: Complete decompression can remove pressure limiting bleeding and abruptly increase arterial pressure. This differs from a selected minimal rescue bridge and is not the preferred sequence before available definitive repair.

questions.question: Despite analgesia and controlled HR/BP, a patient with acute type B dissection develops rising lactate, abdominal pain and reduced superior mesenteric artery perfusion. The anatomy is suitable for endovascular treatment. What is the best next strategy?
options: Continue anti-impulse therapy with repeat imaging in one week
Urgent TEVAR-based repair with assessment of residual branch malperfusion
Isolated superior mesenteric thrombolysis without aortic treatment
Routine open descending replacement as the preferred first procedure
questions.explanation:
Complicated Type B Aortic Dissection

Correct answer: Urgent TEVAR-based repair with assessment of residual branch malperfusion

Recognize Complication

**Malperfusion, rupture, extension, progressive enlargement, refractory pain or uncontrolled BP** require escalation.

Normal arm pressure does not establish visceral perfusion; monitor lactate and organ function.

Restore Flow

**TEVAR covers the proximal tear** and expands the true lumen when anatomy permits.

**Check branch vessels after aortic treatment.**

Static obstruction may persist and need fenestration or branch intervention; bowel viability may require surgical assessment.

**Continue anti-impulse therapy and surveillance.**

Intervention does not remove every residual dissected segment or future aneurysm risk.

Continue anti-impulse therapy with repeat imaging in one week: Medical management is initial treatment for uncomplicated disease; evolving mesenteric ischemia demands urgent intervention rather than scheduled surveillance.

Isolated superior mesenteric thrombolysis without aortic treatment: Thrombolysis treats selected thrombotic occlusions; flap-related malperfusion requires correcting aortic/branch anatomy and carries bleeding concerns.

Routine open descending replacement as the preferred first procedure: Open repair remains important when endovascular treatment is unsuitable or fails; suitable complicated type B anatomy generally favors TEVAR.

questions.question: A stable patient with acute type B dissection has no pain, rupture or organ malperfusion after treatment. CTA shows total aortic diameter 43 mm and false-lumen diameter 24 mm. Which statement best reflects the 2022 ACC/AHA approach?
options: These are high-risk imaging features; selected pre-emptive endovascular management may be considered
These measurements establish rupture and mandate immediate open repair
These measurements prove branch malperfusion and require branch stenting
These measurements have no role until chronic diameter reaches 55 mm
questions.explanation:
High-Risk Uncomplicated Type B Dissection

Correct answer: These are high-risk imaging features; selected pre-emptive endovascular management may be considered

Risk Features

**Examples:** maximal aorta ==>40 mm==; false lumen ==>20–22 mm==; entry tear ==>10 mm==.

Other findings include lesser-curvature entry, interval enlargement, bloody effusion or imaging-only malperfusion.

Qualified Intervention

**Initially uncomplicated does not mean low long-term risk.**

Selected TEVAR can be considered after expert assessment; it is not mandatory for every uncomplicated case.

**Balance remodeling benefit against procedural risk.**

Consider landing zones, connective-tissue disease, stroke/spinal injury risk and follow-up capacity; continue medical treatment whichever pathway is chosen.

These measurements establish rupture and mandate immediate open repair: Rupture requires hemorrhage or other rupture evidence; enlargement markers alone identify risk, not established rupture.

These measurements prove branch malperfusion and require branch stenting: Branch malperfusion depends on vascular and organ findings; the patient has no supplied perfusion deficit.

These measurements have no role until chronic diameter reaches 55 mm: High-risk acute morphology can inform earlier multidisciplinary decisions; chronic aneurysm thresholds do not exhaust the acute assessment.

questions.question: Noncontrast CT shows crescentic hyperattenuating thickening of the ascending aortic wall. Contrast imaging shows no opacified false lumen or visible intimal flap. Which diagnosis best fits?
options: Type A intramural hematoma
Penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer
Aortic pseudoaneurysm
Uncomplicated mural thrombus
questions.explanation:
Aortic Intramural Hematoma

Correct answer: Type A intramural hematoma

Imaging Pattern

**Intramural blood without a perfused false lumen** can produce acute aortic syndrome.

Absence of a visible flap does not make the lesion benign; progression to dissection or rupture can occur.

Management by Location

**Ascending involvement generally prompts urgent surgical management.**

Selected high-operative-risk type A cases without high-risk imaging may be managed expectantly in expert centers, not by routine outpatient observation.

**Uncomplicated type B IMH can start with medical treatment.**

Complications or high-risk progression change the intervention threshold; noncontrast and contrast CT provide complementary information.

Penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer: An ulcer is a focal contrast-filled crater penetrating atherosclerotic intima; the supplied lesion is crescentic mural blood without that crater.

Aortic pseudoaneurysm: Pseudoaneurysm is a contained wall disruption with an outpouching communicating with the lumen; no focal outpouching is described.

Uncomplicated mural thrombus: Luminal thrombus lies within the intimal boundary and usually lacks the characteristic acute hyperattenuating intramural crescent.

questions.question: After successful proximal repair of type A dissection, a patient has a residual dissected descending aorta. Which CT/MRI schedule is recommended by the 2022 ACC/AHA guideline if findings remain stable?
options: At 12 months, then only for recurrent symptoms
At 6 months, then every three years
At 1, 6 and 12 months, then annually
Every month for the first year, then every five years
questions.explanation:
Surveillance After Aortic Dissection

Correct answer: At 1, 6 and 12 months, then annually

Why Follow-up Continues

**Repair treats the immediate segment, not the entire aortopathy.**

Residual false-lumen flow, distal expansion and new aneurysm formation may require later intervention.

Long-Term Care

**CT or MRI at 1, 6, 12 months and annually if stable.**

New symptoms or growth require earlier evaluation; compare consistent measurement planes and techniques.

**Continue BP/heart-rate control**, commonly beta-blockade with additional agents as needed.

**Assess familial disease and counsel activity.**

Screen relatives when appropriate; avoid intense isometric strain and individualize aerobic activity and pregnancy planning.

At 12 months, then only for recurrent symptoms: Aortic enlargement may be asymptomatic; symptom-driven imaging misses progressive residual disease after proximal repair.

At 6 months, then every three years: Long intervals may suit selected small stable aneurysms; residual dissection requires earlier and continuing annual cross-sectional assessment.

Every month for the first year, then every five years: Monthly imaging is not the standard stable follow-up schedule, and five-year intervals are too long for residual dissection.

questions.question: A 42-year-old has a root aneurysm and a father who died from aortic dissection. A multigene panel finds no pathogenic variant. What should be offered to first-degree relatives?
options: Aortic imaging despite the negative genetic panel
Imaging only if a relative develops hypertension
Cascade testing of a variant of uncertain significance as a definitive risk classifier
No screening because the genetic panel excludes inherited disease
questions.explanation:
Family Screening in Thoracic Aortic Disease

Correct answer: Aortic imaging despite the negative genetic panel

Genetic Evaluation

**Young presentation, syndromic features or family history** support genetic counseling and testing.

A pathogenic/likely pathogenic variant enables targeted cascade testing; a VUS requires cautious interpretation.

Imaging Relatives

**Screen first-degree relatives with TTE**, adding CT/MRI when the root or ascending aorta is incompletely seen.

**Negative genetic testing does not exclude heritability.**

Determine repeat imaging from age, baseline dimensions and family events.

**Recognize gene–phenotype patterns:** FBN1 in Marfan; TGFBR1/2 in Loeys–Dietz; COL3A1 in vascular Ehlers–Danlos; ACTA2 in nonsyndromic familial disease.

Imaging only if a relative develops hypertension: Hypertension raises risk but is not required for familial thoracic aortopathy; waiting for it can miss silent dilation.

Cascade testing of a variant of uncertain significance as a definitive risk classifier: A VUS does not establish a disease-causing genotype and should not replace phenotype-based family imaging.

No screening because the genetic panel excludes inherited disease: Current panels do not identify every causal variant; a negative result cannot negate the strongly suggestive family history.

questions.question: A 67-year-old man with a 30-pack-year smoking history, now abstinent, has no abdominal symptoms and no prior aortic imaging. What screening test is appropriate?
options: Contrast abdominal CT as the initial screening test
One-time abdominal aortic ultrasound
Abdominal MRI every year beginning now
No screening after smoking cessation
questions.explanation:
Screening for Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm

Correct answer: One-time abdominal aortic ultrasound

Eligibility

**Men aged ≥65 who have ever smoked** are a standard ACC/AHA screening group.

Family history also informs screening; other organizations specify different age windows and selective eligibility.

Interpret and Act

**AAA is conventionally diameter ==≥3.0 cm==.**

Document maximal diameter with a consistent measurement convention; body size and morphology can modify clinical interpretation.

**Ultrasound is first-line for screening and surveillance.**

Use CT when ultrasound is inadequate or detailed anatomy is needed.

**Screening is preventive, not an emergency pathway.**

Pain, shock or suspected rupture requires immediate clinical/vascular assessment rather than routine screening scheduling.

Contrast abdominal CT as the initial screening test: CTA is valuable for symptomatic disease and repair planning; ultrasound provides screening without contrast or radiation.

Abdominal MRI every year beginning now: MRI can characterize aortic disease but is unnecessary as repeated screening in an otherwise eligible unscreened asymptomatic patient.

No screening after smoking cessation: Ever-smoking remains an eligibility factor; cessation improves risk but does not erase the accumulated aneurysm risk.

questions.question: An asymptomatic woman has a stable fusiform infrarenal AAA measuring 4.6 cm, with no rapid growth. Under the 2022 ACC/AHA framework, what is the usual ultrasound surveillance interval?
options: Every 12 months
Every 3 years
Every 6 months
Every 24 months
questions.explanation:
Sex-Specific AAA Surveillance

Correct answer: Every 6 months

Surveillance

**Sex-specific intervals reflect different rupture risks at a given diameter.**

This ==4.6 cm== aneurysm falls in the six-month group, not the male ==4.0–4.9 cm== annual group.

Change the Plan When Needed

**New attributable pain or rapid enlargement** triggers earlier evaluation, regardless of the scheduled interval.

**Use reproducible measurements.**

Small differences between modalities or planes may reflect technique; confirm clinically important growth.

**Treat vascular risk:** smoking cessation, BP control and atherosclerotic risk reduction; these do not replace surveillance.

Diameter | Interval

3.0–3.9 cm, either sex | 3 years

Men 4.0–4.9; women 4.0–4.4 cm | 1 year

Men ≥5.0; women ≥4.5 cm | 6 months

Every 12 months: Annual imaging applies to women with 4.0–4.4 cm AAA; women at 4.5 cm or greater need shorter surveillance.

Every 3 years: Three-year surveillance applies to uncomplicated 3.0–3.9 cm AAA; this lesion is substantially closer to the female repair threshold.

Every 24 months: Two-year intervals are not the recommended schedule for a woman with a 4.6 cm AAA approaching intervention size.

Symptoms attributable to the aneurysm, rapid growth or unstable morphology can justify earlier repair.

**CTA defines neck, visceral branches and iliac access.**

Plan combined valve and root replacement

Addressing Aortic Disease During Valve Surgery

Correct answer: Assessment for concomitant replacement of the enlarged ascending aorta

Concomitant Aortic Surgery

**2025 ESC/EACTS:** when aortic valve surgery is indicated and surgical risk is low, consider root/ascending replacement at maximal diameter ≥45 mm.

**The 48 mm ascending aorta crosses that concomitant threshold.** This is not a universal threshold for isolated sporadic aortic surgery.

Match the Operation to Anatomy

**Measure root and tubular ascending aorta separately.** Ascending dilation alone does not prove root disease.

**Choose repair or replacement by segment, valve pathology and durability.** Suitable pliable cusps with root disease may permit valve-sparing surgery at an experienced center.

**Consider etiology, growth, body size and family history.** Continue aortic surveillance after valve or aortic surgery because untreated segments remain at risk.

Family dissection, rapid growth and adverse root/aortic morphology inform individualized decisions.

Correct answer: Culture-directed prolonged IV antibiotics plus urgent aortic repair assessment

Diagnosis

**Infective aortitis/aneurysm:** bacteremia plus compatible wall or periaortic changes.

Salmonella and S. aureus are important causes; obtain cultures and assess other infectious foci.

Management

**Antibiotics and aortic source control are coordinated.**

Prolonged IV therapy is generally at least six weeks, individualized by organism, repair and persistent infection.

**Repair timing and technique depend on instability and anatomy.**

Open debridement/reconstruction or selected endovascular bridging/treatment needs expert discussion; infection surveillance remains essential.

**“Mycotic” does not mean fungal**; most such aneurysms are bacterial.

High-dose glucocorticoids for presumed sterile inflammatory aneurysm: Sterile periaortitis can require immunosuppression; bacteremia and an evolving saccular lesion favor infection, which steroids could worsen.

Correct answer: Type Ia endoleak; prompt correction of the proximal seal

**Attachment-site leaks transmit systemic pressure to the sac.**

Type Ia is proximal, Ib distal; prompt repair is needed because successful graft deployment has not excluded the aneurysm.

Comparison and Follow-up

**Type II:** retrograde lumbar/IMA flow; stable sacs can be observed, enlargement prompts reassessment/intervention.

**Type III:** component separation or fabric failure; also a high-pressure leak requiring correction.

**Type IV:** porosity; **type V:** endotension without identified leak.

Surveillance assesses sac size, migration and graft integrity, not merely the presence of contrast.

Type IV endoleak; expect spontaneous resolution of graft porosity: Type IV arises through porous graft material, usually early; a discrete proximal attachment leak indicates failed seal.

Type II endoleak; surveillance if the sac is stable: Type II reflects retrograde collateral filling, not direct inflow at the graft attachment site described here.

Type V endoleak; investigate occult sac pressurization: Type V is sac expansion without a demonstrable leak; visible direct proximal inflow establishes another mechanism.

questions.question: A 70-year-old man has new persistent abdominal and back pain, a tender 4.8 cm infrarenal AAA and no alternative cause on CTA. There is no free rupture and he is stable. What is the best next step?
options: Admit for urgent vascular repair assessment and monitored optimization
Continue six-month ultrasound surveillance because diameter is below 5.5 cm
Treat pain and reassess after a routine outpatient interval
Begin therapeutic anticoagulation for mural thrombus as the principal treatment
questions.explanation:
Symptomatic AAA Below the Elective Size Threshold

Correct answer: Admit for urgent vascular repair assessment and monitored optimization

Symptomatic Disease

**Attributable pain or tenderness warrants repair evaluation irrespective of usual elective diameter.**

Exclude alternative diagnoses, contained rupture and infection; absence of free rupture does not establish benign disease.

**Suspected rupture:** new abdominal/back pain with hypotension, sometimes a pulsatile mass.

The complete triad is often absent; unstable patients need immediate vascular resuscitation and repair planning, not delay for routine surveillance imaging.

Immediate Care

**Monitor, control pain and BP, and involve the vascular team.**

Stable patients permit rapid anatomical planning and optimization; deterioration requires emergency intervention.

**CTA defines anatomy and complications.**

Aneurysm-related embolization, fistulation or rapid growth can also justify intervention below standard fusiform thresholds.

**Long-term care continues after repair:** tobacco cessation, cardiovascular prevention and procedure-specific surveillance.

Continue six-month ultrasound surveillance because diameter is below 5.5 cm: Size-based surveillance applies to asymptomatic stable aneurysms; new attributable pain changes the repair indication.

Treat pain and reassess after a routine outpatient interval: Analgesia is supportive but does not remove the risk signaled by a newly symptomatic aneurysm; inpatient urgent evaluation is needed.

Begin therapeutic anticoagulation for mural thrombus as the principal treatment: Mural thrombus is common within AAA; it is not by itself an indication for anticoagulation or an explanation permitting delayed repair assessment.

ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001106

questions.question: Right and left brachial systolic pressures are 150 and 140 mmHg. Right dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pressures are 90 and 105 mmHg. What is the right ABI?
questions.explanation:
Calculating the Ankle–Brachial Index

Correct answer: 0.70

Calculation

**ABI = higher ankle artery pressure / higher brachial pressure.**

Right ABI = max(90,105)/max(150,140) = 105/150 = **0.70**.

Interpretation

**ABI ≤0.90 is abnormal** and supports PAD in the appropriate clinical setting.

**Calculate each leg separately**, using the same higher-arm denominator.

Use standardized supine Doppler measurements; subclavian disease or noncompressible ankle arteries can complicate interpretation.

**ABI alone does not establish CLTI.**

Rest pain, nonhealing tissue loss and objective perfusion assessment determine limb threat.

ABI | Category

≤0.90 | Abnormal

0.91–0.99 | Borderline

1.00–1.40 | Normal

>1.40 | Noncompressible

questions.question: A patient has reproducible calf discomfort while walking, relieved within minutes of stopping. Resting ABI is 1.06. What is the next physiological test?
options: Treadmill exercise ABI
Toe–brachial index as the primary next test
CT angiography before physiological confirmation
Repeat resting ABI in one year
questions.explanation:
Exercise ABI for Exertional Symptoms

Correct answer: Treadmill exercise ABI

Reveal Reduced Flow Reserve

**Exercise increases demand**, exposing a pressure drop across flow-limiting stenoses that may be unapparent at rest.

**Use exercise ABI when symptoms suggest PAD and resting ABI is >0.90 to ≤1.40.**

Interpret with the Protocol

**Assess postexercise ankle pressure, ABI and recovery**, together with reproduction of symptoms.

A ==>20%== ABI fall or ==>30 mmHg== ankle-pressure fall is used in some protocols; criteria vary and are not interchangeable universal rules.

**A normal test prompts alternative diagnoses**, including spinal stenosis and musculoskeletal disease; persistent uncertainty may warrant further vascular assessment.

Toe–brachial index as the primary next test: TBI is particularly useful for noncompressible ankle arteries or suspected CLTI; a normal compressible resting ABI with exertional symptoms favors exercise testing.

CT angiography before physiological confirmation: CTA defines anatomy when intervention is contemplated or testing is inconclusive; exercise ABI is the appropriate next physiological study here.

Repeat resting ABI in one year: Surveillance suits established stable disease; it does not resolve current symptoms that may reveal obstruction only during exercise.

ACC/AHA Lower Extremity PAD Guideline, 2024 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001251

questions.question: A patient with diabetes and CKD has a nonhealing toe ulcer, weak pedal pulses and ABI 1.62. Which physiological test is most useful next?
options: Repeat ABI using a higher cuff inflation pressure alone
Toe pressure and toe–brachial index with waveforms
Exercise ABI as the sole next study
Venous reflux ultrasonography
questions.explanation:
Noncompressible Ankle Arteries

Correct answer: Toe pressure and toe–brachial index with waveforms

Why ABI Misleads

**Medial calcification in diabetes/CKD** can make ankle arteries poorly compressible and elevate ABI.

A high ABI is not proof of excellent perfusion.

Digital Perfusion

**TBI ≤0.70 is abnormal.**

Digital arteries are generally less affected by noncompressibility; obtain toe waveforms as well as pressure.

**Toe pressure ==<30 mmHg== suggests severe ischemia** and poor healing potential.

**Use TcPO₂ or skin perfusion pressure when toe testing is unavailable or unreliable.**

Combine perfusion, wound and infection assessment; urgently evaluate possible CLTI rather than dismissing the ulcer because ABI is high.

Repeat ABI using a higher cuff inflation pressure alone: Calcified arteries resist compression; greater cuff pressure does not reliably restore diagnostic accuracy or assess digital perfusion.

Exercise ABI as the sole next study: Exercise ABI addresses exertional symptoms with compressible arteries; tissue loss and noncompressibility require toe/local perfusion assessment.

Venous reflux ultrasonography: Venous testing suits edema and typical venous ulceration; it does not resolve suspected arterial ischemia with a falsely high ABI.

questions.question: A patient has a painful forefoot ulcer for six weeks, worse pain with elevation, ABI 0.83 and toe pressure 24 mmHg. Which interpretation is best?
options: Acute limb ischemia because toe pressure is below 30 mmHg
Claudication alone because ABI is above 0.50
Neuropathic ulceration alone because the ABI is only mildly abnormal
CLTI is supported despite an ABI that is not profoundly reduced
questions.explanation:
Chronic Limb-Threatening Ischemia

Correct answer: CLTI is supported despite an ABI that is not profoundly reduced

Clinical and Perfusion Criteria

**Objectively documented PAD plus rest pain, gangrene or ulceration >2 weeks** supports CLTI.

ABI can underestimate severity, particularly with calcification or distal disease.

**Toe pressure ==24 mmHg== is severely reduced.**

TcPO₂ and skin perfusion pressure can supplement assessment; thresholds predict probability, not certainty, of healing.

Limb-Salvage Care

**Prompt vascular/multidisciplinary evaluation** for revascularization, infection treatment and wound care.

**Offload wounds and manage systemic risk**, including smoking, lipids and diabetes.

Perfusion restoration alone does not replace debridement, infection control or preventive foot care.

Acute limb ischemia because toe pressure is below 30 mmHg: ALI is defined by abrupt deterioration, generally under two weeks; a six-week wound with chronic symptoms fits a chronic limb-threat pathway.

Claudication alone because ABI is above 0.50: Claudication is exertional discomfort without ischemic rest pain or tissue loss; the persistent ulcer and severely reduced toe pressure indicate greater limb threat.

Neuropathic ulceration alone because the ABI is only mildly abnormal: Neuropathy may coexist, but low digital pressure and elevation-related pain establish an important ischemic component requiring vascular evaluation.

questions.question: A smoker has exertional buttock and thigh pain, reduced femoral pulses and erectile dysfunction. Which arterial distribution best explains the findings?
options: Isolated popliteal artery entrapment
Isolated superficial femoral artery disease
Isolated tibial arterial disease
Aortoiliac occlusive disease
questions.explanation:
Localizing Chronic Arterial Occlusion

Correct answer: Aortoiliac occlusive disease

Anatomical Pattern

**Leriche pattern:** aortoiliac obstruction with proximal claudication, reduced femoral pulses and erectile dysfunction.

Symptoms depend on collateral flow and activity; not every patient has the complete triad.

Assessment and Treatment

**Confirm PAD physiologically**, then map anatomy with duplex/CTA/MRA when revascularization is being considered.

**Risk-factor treatment and structured exercise** remain fundamental.

**Revascularization depends on symptoms, anatomy and operative risk.**

Endovascular repair or aortobifemoral bypass may be appropriate; the classic syndrome name alone does not dictate one procedure.

Isolated popliteal artery entrapment: Entrapment can cause exertional calf ischemia, especially in younger active patients; it does not typically produce bilateral pelvic-inflow symptoms.

Isolated superficial femoral artery disease: Femoropopliteal obstruction commonly causes calf claudication with preserved femoral inflow; it does not explain the full proximal-pulse and pelvic symptom pattern.

Isolated tibial arterial disease: Tibial disease chiefly affects distal foot perfusion, often in diabetes; it would not account for reduced femoral pulses.

ACC/AHA Lower Extremity PAD Guideline, 2024 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001251

questions.question: An older adult develops bilateral buttock and leg discomfort while standing or walking. Sitting or bending forward relieves symptoms; simply standing still does not. Pedal pulses and resting/exercise ABI are normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Aortoiliac occlusive disease
Lumbar spinal stenosis
Chronic venous outflow obstruction
Hip osteoarthritis
questions.explanation:
Vascular Versus Neurogenic Claudication

Correct answer: Lumbar spinal stenosis

Discriminating Features

**Neurogenic symptoms depend on lumbar posture.**

Flexion can enlarge the spinal canal; walking distance may vary and cycling may be better tolerated.

**Vascular claudication tracks muscle demand.**

It is often reproducible and resolves after stopping without a specific spinal position.

Avoid False Dichotomies

**Spinal and vascular disease can coexist.**

A normal resting ABI alone would not exclude PAD; here normal exercise physiology also supports the alternative.

**Neurological examination and appropriate spinal imaging** follow the clinical assessment; assess red flags urgently when present.

Aortoiliac occlusive disease: Aortoiliac disease can cause proximal exertional pain, but vascular pain generally improves with rest without requiring flexion and often has abnormal pulse/physiological findings.

Chronic venous outflow obstruction: Venous claudication causes bursting discomfort and swelling, often relieved by elevation; the posture-dependent flexion pattern is more characteristic of spinal stenosis.

Hip osteoarthritis: Hip disease causes joint-related pain and restricted movement; the supplied bilateral posture-dependent leg syndrome with walking favors neurogenic claudication.

ACC/AHA Lower Extremity PAD Guideline, 2024 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001251

questions.question: A patient with symptomatic PAD takes atorvastatin 80 mg daily with good adherence. LDL cholesterol remains 88 mg/dL. Under the 2024 ACC/AHA PAD guideline, which strategy is appropriate?
options: Reduce atorvastatin because LDL is below 100 mg/dL
Add ezetimibe or a PCSK9 inhibitor to maximally tolerated statin therapy
Replace atorvastatin with fibrate monotherapy
Continue statin alone until LDL exceeds 130 mg/dL
questions.explanation:
Lipid Lowering in Symptomatic PAD

Correct answer: Add ezetimibe or a PCSK9 inhibitor to maximally tolerated statin therapy

Treatment Target

**High-intensity statin aims for ==≥50%== LDL reduction.**

Atorvastatin ==40–80 mg== or rosuvastatin ==20–40 mg== daily are standard options.

**2024 ACC/AHA PAD:** adding ezetimibe or a PCSK9 inhibitor is reasonable when LDL remains ==≥70 mg/dL== on maximal tolerated statin.

Monitor and Individualize

**Confirm adherence, tolerance and secondary causes** before escalating.

questions.question: A patient with symptomatic PAD has aspirin-induced urticaria, no recent revascularization and no separate anticoagulation indication. Which long-term antithrombotic regimen is most appropriate?
options: Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily alone
Ticagrelor 90 mg twice daily

questions.explanation:
Single Antiplatelet Therapy for PAD

Correct answer: Clopidogrel 75 mg daily

Why Clopidogrel

**Single antiplatelet therapy reduces cardiovascular risk in symptomatic PAD.**

Clopidogrel ==75 mg== daily is an appropriate aspirin alternative; aspirin is another standard agent when tolerated.

Choose Intensity Deliberately

**Dual-pathway inhibition requires both vascular-dose rivaroxaban and low-dose aspirin**, with acceptable bleeding risk.

**Recent procedures or another anticoagulation indication change the regimen.**

Avoid simply stacking agents; assess bleeding, interactions and duration.

**Antiplatelet therapy does not directly restore walking flow reserve**; combine prevention with exercise and symptom-directed treatment.

questions.question: Following lower-extremity revascularization, a patient has low bleeding risk, preserved renal function and no AF or VTE. Which long-term regimen has evidence for reducing cardiovascular and major limb events?
options: Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus low-dose aspirin
Rivaroxaban 20 mg daily plus aspirin
Clopidogrel plus aspirin indefinitely for every such patient
Dabigatran 150 mg twice daily plus aspirin
questions.explanation:

Regimen and Evidence

**Rivaroxaban ==2.5 mg== twice daily + aspirin ==75–100 mg== daily** is the dual-pathway regimen.

**Check bleeding risk, renal/hepatic function and interacting drugs.**

Only the first 24 hours
1–6 months
Lifelong regardless of bleeding risk
questions.explanation:
DAPT After Endovascular PAD Treatment

Correct answer: 1–6 months

**DAPT with a P2Y12 inhibitor and low-dose aspirin for 1–6 months is reasonable** after endovascular revascularization.

Choose duration by procedure, ischemic risk, bleeding and other antithrombotic indications.

**DAPT and dual-pathway inhibition are different strategies.**

**A separate coronary stent or AF indication** requires coordinated planning across vascular and cardiac care.

At least 18–24 months in every patient: Prolonged DAPT may be required for a separate indication, but that duration is not routinely mandated by peripheral intervention.

Only the first 24 hours: Periprocedural therapy alone is shorter than the guideline-supported range when DAPT is chosen after endovascular revascularization.

questions.question: A patient with limiting claudication despite structured exercise has no heart failure but takes diltiazem. If cilostazol is prescribed, which regimen best follows its labeling?
options: 100 mg once daily with the largest meal
100 mg twice daily without dose adjustment
50 mg twice daily, separated from meals
200 mg twice daily to overcome the interaction
questions.explanation:
Cilostazol Dose and Interactions

Correct answer: 50 mg twice daily, separated from meals

Mechanism and Dosing

**PDE3 inhibition improves walking symptoms** through antiplatelet and vasodilator effects.

Usual dose: ==100 mg== twice daily, ≥30 minutes before or ≥2 hours after meals.

**Reduce to ==50 mg== twice daily** with strong/moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors or CYP2C19 inhibitors.

Examples include diltiazem and omeprazole.

Safety and Follow-up

**Contraindicated in heart failure of any severity.**

Headache, diarrhea and palpitations are common; assess benefit over several weeks and discontinue if ineffective after an adequate trial.

**Cilostazol is symptom therapy**, not a replacement for cardiovascular prevention; pentoxifylline is not recommended for claudication.

100 mg once daily with the largest meal: Once-daily dosing is not the standard interaction-adjusted regimen; food can increase exposure, so the label advises separation from meals.

100 mg twice daily without dose adjustment: One hundred milligrams twice daily is the usual dose without relevant inhibitors; diltiazem inhibits CYP3A4 and increases exposure.

200 mg twice daily to overcome the interaction: Enzyme inhibition increases rather than decreases cilostazol exposure; escalation would raise adverse-effect risk instead of compensating for reduced efficacy.

ACC/AHA Lower Extremity PAD Guideline, 2024 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001251

questions.question: A patient with stable claudication asks for an evidence-based walking program. Which prescription best matches standard supervised exercise therapy?
options: Intermittent walking for 30–45 active minutes, at least 3 times weekly for at least 12 weeks
Continuous pain-free walking for 10 minutes twice weekly for 4 weeks
Lower-limb resistance training alone as the initial rehabilitation program
Self-directed walking advice with reassessment after six months
questions.explanation:

Correct answer: Intermittent walking for 30–45 active minutes, at least 3 times weekly for at least 12 weeks

Program Design

**Walk to moderate or moderately severe claudication, then rest and repeat.**

Active exercise time builds toward 30–45 minutes; sessions also include warm-up and cool-down.

**Minimum typical course:** ≥3 sessions/week for ≥12 weeks.

Implementation

**Structured community/home programs are alternatives** when supervised access is limited.

Use coaching, monitoring and progression; a casual instruction to walk is not equivalent.

**Screen for exercise-limiting cardiac or musculoskeletal disease.**

Rest pain, tissue loss or acute ischemia requires a different assessment; do not apply a claudication exercise prescription to an unstable threatened limb.

Continuous pain-free walking for 10 minutes twice weekly for 4 weeks: Lower-intensity activity can help conditioning, but this prescription is shorter and less frequent than the standard supervised claudication program.

Lower-limb resistance training alone as the initial rehabilitation program: Resistance exercise may complement rehabilitation or suit selected limitations; interval walking is the standard supervised program for ambulatory claudication.

Self-directed walking advice with reassessment after six months: General advice is helpful but differs from supervised or structured home-based programs that include behavioral support, progression and follow-up.

questions.question: A patient remains unable to perform essential daily activities after guideline-directed medical therapy and a completed structured exercise program. Hemodynamically significant femoropopliteal disease is confirmed. What is the appropriate next step?
options: Continue medical treatment until gangrene develops
Discuss revascularization to improve function and quality of life
Perform bypass solely to prevent future progression in every claudicant
Use angiography to choose a procedure without discussing durability or reintervention
questions.explanation:
When to Revascularize Claudication

Correct answer: Discuss revascularization to improve function and quality of life

Selection

**Confirm symptoms are vascular and important to the patient.**

Revascularization is reasonable after inadequate response to medical treatment including structured exercise.

Procedure and Follow-up

**Endovascular versus surgery depends on anatomy, conduit and risk.**

Autogenous vein is generally preferred for suitable femoropopliteal bypass.

**Discuss durability and reintervention**, especially in long or heavily calcified lesions.

**Continue prevention and exercise after the procedure.**

Revascularization improves local flow but does not cure systemic atherosclerosis or remove the need for antithrombotic and lipid therapy.

Continue medical treatment until gangrene develops: Tissue loss is not required for symptom-directed revascularization; persistent functionally limiting claudication after appropriate therapy is a valid indication.

Perform bypass solely to prevent future progression in every claudicant: Routine prophylactic revascularization is not the indication; here the rationale is current disability despite conservative treatment.

Use angiography to choose a procedure without discussing durability or reintervention: Anatomy matters, but shared decisions must include expected functional benefit, procedural risk, durability and potential repeat interventions.

questions.question: A diabetic patient has a foot ulcer, toe pressure 25 mmHg and spreading local infection. Which framework most directly combines the three domains needed to estimate threatened-limb severity?
options: Rutherford acute ischemia category
Fontaine classification
Rutherford chronic PAD category
WIfI classification
questions.explanation:
WIfI Staging of a Threatened Limb

Correct answer: WIfI classification

Three Domains

**Wound, Ischemia, foot Infection** are each graded 0–3.

The combined pattern informs amputation risk and likely benefit from revascularization, alongside anatomy and patient risk.

Clinical Use

**Toe pressure ==<30 mmHg== corresponds to severe ischemia** in the usual WIfI grading.

**Do not infer a complete WIfI stage from one number.**

Wound depth/extent and infection severity must also be recorded.

**Treat infection and ischemia together.**

Urgent drainage/debridement may be necessary; staged reconstruction and revascularization depend on systemic stability and foot viability.

WIfI ischemia grade | Toe pressure/TcPO₂, mmHg

0 | ≥60

1 | 40–59

2 | 30–39

3 | <30

Rutherford acute ischemia category: The acute scheme classifies viability using sensory/motor deficits and Doppler signals; it is not the chronic wound–infection framework.

Fontaine classification: Fontaine broadly groups asymptomatic disease, claudication, rest pain and tissue loss; it does not separately grade wound, ischemia and infection.

Rutherford chronic PAD category: Chronic Rutherford categories describe symptom/tissue-loss severity but do not provide the same separate infection and physiological grading.

questions.question: A patient with six hours of limb ischemia has sensory loss limited to the toes, no motor deficit, absent arterial Doppler signal and preserved venous signal. Which Rutherford category applies?
options: IIb: immediately threatened
I: viable
IIa: marginally threatened
III: irreversible
questions.explanation:
Rutherford Acute Limb Ischemia Classification

Correct answer: IIa: marginally threatened

Bedside Viability

**IIa is salvageable with prompt treatment.**

Motor function is preserved; sensory change is limited, and venous flow remains detectable.

Act on the Category

**Give heparin unless contraindicated and obtain urgent vascular assessment.**

Expedited imaging can guide treatment if it does not delay salvage.

**Repeat neurological and Doppler examination.**

Progression to motor weakness changes the urgency; symptom duration alone does not establish viability.

Category | Sensory/motor findings | Doppler

I | No loss/weakness | Arterial +; venous +

IIa | Toe sensory loss; no weakness | Arterial often −; venous +

IIb | Beyond toes; mild/moderate weakness | Arterial −; venous +

III | Profound anesthesia; paralysis/rigor | Arterial −; venous −

IIb: immediately threatened: IIb generally includes sensory loss beyond the toes and mild/moderate weakness; neither is supplied in this case.

I: viable: Category I has no sensory or motor loss and audible arterial/venous signals; toe sensory loss with absent arterial flow exceeds that category.

III: irreversible: Irreversible ischemia has profound anesthesia and paralysis/rigor, generally with absent arterial and venous signals; those findings are absent here.

questions.question: A patient has an acutely cold painful foot from suspected arterial occlusion. There is no active bleeding, HIT history or evidence of aortic dissection. While urgent vascular treatment is arranged, what should be started?
options: Warfarin without parenteral anticoagulation
Aspirin alone while waiting for angiographic confirmation
Systemic intravenous unfractionated heparin
Low-dose rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily
questions.explanation:
Initial Anticoagulation in Acute Limb Ischemia

Correct answer: Systemic intravenous unfractionated heparin

Purpose

**UFH limits thrombus propagation and further embolization.**

Its rapid onset, short half-life and reversibility suit urgent procedural care; it does not by itself guarantee reperfusion.

Administration and Exceptions

**Use an institutional IV protocol with laboratory-guided titration.**

ESVS describes an initial 5,000 IU or 70–100 IU/kg bolus, followed by infusion adjusted to response and ACT/aPTT; procedural/thrombolysis regimens differ.

**Check bleeding, platelets and contraindications.**

HIT requires a non-heparin strategy; suspected dissection or major bleeding changes the immediate plan.

**Do not delay vascular assessment or revascularization** while awaiting anticoagulant effect.

Warfarin without parenteral anticoagulation: Warfarin has delayed onset and may later address an embolic indication; it is unsuitable as sole immediate anticoagulation here.

Aspirin alone while waiting for angiographic confirmation: Antiplatelet therapy may be appropriate for long-term prevention but does not replace immediate systemic anticoagulation in eligible ALI.

Low-dose rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily: The vascular prevention dose is not a treatment regimen for acute arterial occlusion requiring immediate titratable anticoagulation.

ACC/AHA Lower Extremity PAD Guideline, 2024 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001251

options: Primary amputation with subsequent embolic-source investigation
Catheter alteplase infusion with planned next-day angiographic reassessment
Therapeutic heparin with serial examinations before deciding on intervention
Emergency revascularization using the fastest appropriate available strategy
questions.explanation:
Immediately Threatened Limb

Correct answer: Emergency revascularization using the fastest appropriate available strategy

Why Motor Deficit Matters

**Rutherford IIb:** salvageable only with immediate treatment.

Neuromuscular dysfunction indicates severe ischemia; a historical time cutoff cannot substitute for the current examination.

Emergency Sequence

**Anticoagulate if eligible, provide analgesia and mobilize vascular expertise.**

**Choose rapid surgical, endovascular or hybrid reperfusion** by anatomy, cause and local capability.

Slow thrombolysis alone may be inappropriate; selected rapidly initiated catheter strategies can be used by experienced teams.

**Monitor for compartment syndrome and metabolic reperfusion injury**, including potassium, acidosis, CK and renal function.

Recognize IIb → Immediate vascular intervention → Reperfusion and compartment monitoring

Primary amputation with subsequent embolic-source investigation: Mild/moderate weakness with preserved venous signal can be salvageable category IIb; it is not equivalent to fixed paralysis/rigor of category III.

Catheter alteplase infusion with planned next-day angiographic reassessment: Catheter lysis may suit selected salvageable limbs, but motor weakness requires rapid reperfusion; a prolonged infusion with delayed reassessment risks irreversible progression.

Therapeutic heparin with serial examinations before deciding on intervention: Heparin limits propagation but does not reliably remove the occlusion; motor deficit should trigger emergency restoration of flow.

questions.question: A cold mottled limb has fixed anesthesia, rigid paralysis and no arterial or venous Doppler signals on expert assessment. Which strategy is appropriate?
options: Heparin alone with delayed outpatient review
Prolonged catheter thrombolysis to test whether tissue recovers
Emergency bypass to restore flow before reassessing the rigid limb
Primary amputation of nonviable tissue rather than attempted reperfusion
questions.explanation:
Irreversible Limb Ischemia

Correct answer: Primary amputation of nonviable tissue rather than attempted reperfusion

Category III

**Profound anesthesia, fixed paralysis/rigor and absent venous flow** support irreversible ischemia.

The diagnosis requires expert clinical assessment; absent pulses alone are insufficient.

Protect the Patient

**Primary amputation/source control** is indicated when tissue is truly nonviable.

**Resuscitate and monitor potassium, acid–base state and renal function.**

Reperfusion of dead muscle risks hyperkalemia, acidosis, rhabdomyolysis and cardiovascular collapse.

**Plan rehabilitation and prevention**, including contralateral-limb assessment and treatment of the embolic or atherosclerotic cause.

Heparin alone with delayed outpatient review: Anticoagulation cannot reverse necrosis; ongoing nonviable tissue and systemic risk require urgent definitive surgical management.

Prolonged catheter thrombolysis to test whether tissue recovers: Thrombolysis can help salvageable ischemia, but established nonviability will not be reversed and exposes the patient to bleeding and reperfusion toxicity.

Emergency bypass to restore flow before reassessing the rigid limb: Revascularizing irreversibly necrotic muscle can release potassium, acid and myoglobin without salvaging function; confirmed category III should not undergo routine reperfusion.

questions.question: After successful embolectomy, a patient develops escalating calf pain, tense compartments and pain on passive toe movement. Pedal Doppler signals remain present. What is the best next action?
options: Escalate opioid analgesia and wait for pulse loss
Reassurance because arterial Doppler signals are present
Urgent assessment for compartment syndrome and fasciotomy when clinically indicated
Start anticoagulation for presumed DVT without surgical assessment
questions.explanation:
Compartment Syndrome After Revascularization

Correct answer: Urgent assessment for compartment syndrome and fasciotomy when clinically indicated

Recognition

**Reperfusion edema raises pressure within a closed fascial space.**

Disproportionate pain, passive-stretch pain, tension and neurological change are important; pulses may persist.

Treatment

**Urgent surgical decompression** is required when the diagnosis is established.

Pressure measurement can help an uncertain examination but must not delay treatment in a clear clinical syndrome.

**Four-compartment leg fasciotomy** is commonly required; selected high-risk prolonged ischemia may warrant prophylactic fasciotomy.

**Monitor systemic reperfusion injury:** potassium, CK, acidosis, urine output and creatinine; treat abnormalities promptly.

Escalate opioid analgesia and wait for pulse loss: Analgesia is supportive, but waiting for late vascular signs risks irreversible nerve and muscle injury.

Reassurance because arterial Doppler signals are present: Compartment pressure can impair microcirculation despite large-artery flow; palpable pulses or Doppler signals do not exclude compartment syndrome.

Start anticoagulation for presumed DVT without surgical assessment: DVT can cause swelling, but tense compartments and passive-stretch pain after reperfusion demand urgent compartment evaluation before attributing symptoms to venous disease.

questions.question: A patient has acute bypass graft thrombosis with toe-only sensory loss, preserved motor function and venous flow. There is no major bleeding contraindication, and a monitored vascular service can begin treatment promptly. Which approach is reasonable?
options: Systemic full-dose IV thrombolysis as the standard preferred route
Catheter-directed thrombolysis with reassessment and treatment of the underlying lesion
Observation on antiplatelet therapy until the graft recanalizes
Primary amputation because a bypass graft has thrombosed
questions.explanation:
Selecting Catheter-Directed Thrombolysis

Correct answer: Catheter-directed thrombolysis with reassessment and treatment of the underlying lesion

Who May Benefit

**Selected Rutherford IIa limbs** allow time for catheter thrombus treatment when bleeding risk and anatomy are suitable.

IIb requires a faster strategy; III is not a lysis indication.

Protocol and Monitoring

**Alteplase commonly ==0.5–1 mg/hour== intra-arterially** under a specialist protocol.

Dose, duration and concurrent heparin differ from systemic thrombolysis; monitor access bleeding, hemoglobin and clinical perfusion.

**Exclude major contraindications**, including active bleeding and important recent intracranial events.

**Correct the cause of thrombosis**, such as graft anastomotic stenosis, after thrombus clearance; reassess promptly if neurological status worsens.

Systemic full-dose IV thrombolysis as the standard preferred route: Catheter-directed therapy delivers drug into thrombus and is an established selected-limb strategy; systemic thrombolysis is not the preferred ALI approach.

Observation on antiplatelet therapy until the graft recanalizes: A threatened limb requires urgent assessment/reperfusion; spontaneous recanalization cannot be relied upon to preserve tissue.

Primary amputation because a bypass graft has thrombosed: Graft thrombosis does not itself establish nonviability; preserved motor function and limited sensory loss support a salvageable limb.

  • A — Systemic full-dose IV thrombolysis as the standard preferred route: Catheter-directed therapy delivers drug into thrombus and is an established selected-limb strategy; systemic thrombolysis is not the preferred ALI approach.
  • C — Observation on antiplatelet therapy until the graft recanalizes: A threatened limb requires urgent assessment/reperfusion; spontaneous recanalization cannot be relied upon to preserve tissue.
  • D — Primary amputation because a bypass graft has thrombosed: Graft thrombosis does not itself establish nonviability; preserved motor function and limited sensory loss support a salvageable limb.

References

  • ESVS Acute Limb Ischaemia Guideline, 2020
  • ACC/AHA Lower Extremity PAD Guideline, 2024

questions.explanation:
Embolic Versus In-Situ Arterial Occlusion

Correct answer: Cardiac arterial embolism

Clues to the Cause

**Embolism:** abrupt onset, cardiac source, previously asymptomatic limb and relatively normal opposite limb.

These are probabilistic clues; imaging and operative findings establish anatomy.

**Thrombosis:** underlying plaque, prior bypass/stent, aneurysm or a preceding PAD history.

Treat Now, Investigate in Parallel

**Urgent viability assessment, heparin if eligible and reperfusion planning** take priority.

**ECG, echocardiography and rhythm assessment** identify the source without delaying limb salvage.

Long-term anticoagulation is indicated for appropriate AF-related embolism; vascular-dose rivaroxaban plus aspirin is not a substitute for an AF regimen.

Acute thrombosis of advanced chronic multilevel PAD: In-situ thrombosis more often accompanies previous claudication, diffuse disease or abnormal contralateral pulses; the sudden isolated event with AF favors embolism.

Cholesterol crystal embolization: Cholesterol emboli often cause distal blue toes with preserved proximal pulses and systemic small-vessel findings, rather than abrupt major-limb arterial occlusion.

Chronic venous insufficiency: Venous insufficiency produces edema and chronic skin changes, not an abrupt arterial perfusion deficit in the setting of an embolic source.
